Chapter 1

Reading the Land

The Southeastern United States is one of the most physically varied regions in the country.

Mountains. Rolling hills. River valleys. Swamps. Barrier islands. Beaches. Deltas. Fertile plains. Pine forests. Coalfields. Wetlands. Major port cities.

The Southeast holds all of these landscapes inside one . That geography shaped where people lived, what they grew, how they traveled, where cities developed, and how history unfolded across hundreds of years.

There is no single perfect definition of "the Southeast." For this lesson, we study twelve states: Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, and Louisiana.

Chapter 2

What Makes a Region a Region

A is an area that shares certain characteristics. The Southeast is not exactly the same everywhere, but most of it shares a few key things.
  • Humid climate with long, warm growing seasons
  • Major river systems that drain the interior toward the coast
  • Coastal plains on the Atlantic Ocean or Gulf of Mexico
  • Southern Appalachian Mountains running through the interior
  • Forests, wetlands, and fertile farmland
  • A history shaped by agriculture, slavery, the Civil War, and modern growth

In the Southeast, physical geography and human history are tightly connected. The land helped decide where Indigenous nations lived, where colonists settled, where plantations developed, where railroads ran, and where major cities grew.

Physical Region 1

The Appalachian Mountains

The Appalachians are very old mountains. has worn them down for hundreds of millions of years, sending toward the coast.

The Appalachian Mountains run from the northeastern United States down into the Southeast. In our they include the Blue Ridge Mountains, the Great Smoky Mountains, the Ridge and Valley region, and the Appalachian .

Mountains are not just scenery. They affect:

  • Settlement patterns and travel routes
  • What kind of farming is possible
  • Coal mining and timber
  • Where rivers start
  • Cultural patterns in isolated valleys

Mountain land is harder to farm than flat land, but mountain valleys often have fertile soil. Mountain gaps, like the Cumberland Gap, became some of the most important transportation routes in early American history.

Physical Region 2

The Piedmont

means "foot of the mountain." It is a broad belt of rolling hills between the high Appalachians and the flat .

The stretches across Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Alabama. The land here rolls, dips, and rises like waves. It is not flat, but it is not steep either.

The Piedmont became important because of one boundary line: the . Rivers flowing out of the mountains drop sharply in elevation at the Fall Line, creating waterfalls and rapids.

Before modern power plants, those falling rivers powered mills and factories. Before railroads, boats from the coast could only travel inland as far as the Fall Line. So cities grew exactly there:

  • Richmond, Virginia
  • Raleigh, North Carolina
  • Columbia, South Carolina
  • Augusta, Georgia
  • Macon, Georgia
  • Columbus, Georgia
  • Montgomery, Alabama
Mini-Lesson

Why the Fall Line Matters

The is one of the best examples in all of geography of how the land controls where people build cities.

Picture a river flowing from the mountains toward the ocean. In the highlands, the river flows over hard, ancient crystalline rock. Then it reaches softer, flatter sediments. At that boundary, the river drops suddenly. Rapids and waterfalls form.

That boundary is the .

It mattered for two huge reasons:

  1. Waterpower. Before electricity, factories needed moving water to drive machines. Mills clustered at the Fall Line because rushing water did the work.
  2. End of navigation. Before railroads, boats from the Atlantic could move upstream only until they hit the rapids. The Fall Line marked the last reachable inland port on each river.

Drop one finger on a map at Augusta, Georgia. Slide it north to Columbia, then to Raleigh, then to Richmond. You have traced the Fall Line, and almost every city you touched grew up because of it.

Physical Region 3

The Coastal Plain

The is the low, flat land near the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico. It contains sandy soils, pine forests, wetlands, barrier islands, estuaries, and beaches.

The Southeast contains the largest area of wetlands and the largest coral reef tract in the contiguous United States. Marshes, estuaries, barrier islands, mangroves, swamps, and reefs all show up along these coasts.

The shaped almost every part of southern life:

  • Plantation agriculture in flat, fertile soil
  • Rice, indigo, cotton, tobacco, peanuts, and citrus
  • Port cities at the mouths of major rivers
  • Fishing and shrimping communities along the coast
  • Tourism at beaches and barrier islands
  • Hurricane risk from warm Atlantic and Gulf waters
Physical Region 4

The Mississippi River and Delta

The Mississippi River is one of North America's most important river systems. It drains a huge part of the interior United States.

In the Southeast, the Mississippi most strongly affects Arkansas, Mississippi, and Louisiana. A forms when a river slows down at its mouth and drops , building new land out into the sea.

Louisiana's delta is one of the most important regions in the country. It is also at risk. Levees, canals, hurricanes, sinking land, and reduced sediment delivery all threaten the marshes that protect inland Louisiana from storms.

The river itself helped create:

  • Fertile floodplains for cotton, corn, and soybeans
  • Major trade routes connecting the interior to the Gulf
  • River cities like Memphis, Vicksburg, Baton Rouge, and New Orleans
  • Wetlands and fisheries
  • Serious flood risk that required levees and dams
Physical Region 5

The Floridan Aquifer

An is an underground layer of rock or that stores and moves groundwater. The Floridan aquifer is one of the most productive in the world.

The Floridan system lies beneath all of Florida and parts of Georgia, Alabama, and South Carolina. It supplies drinking water for cities, irrigation water for farms, and the cool, clear water that feeds Florida's famous springs.

Rainwater soaks into the ground, filters down through layers of limestone, and collects in the aquifer. In many places that groundwater rises back to the surface as a spring, then flows into rivers like the Suwannee or the St. Johns.

This invisible system supports:

  • Drinking water for millions of people
  • Farms growing citrus, vegetables, and sugarcane
  • Hundreds of natural springs
  • Wetlands and the Everglades
  • Tourism economies built around clear-water rivers and springs
Region Spotlight

The Everglades and Florida Wetlands

South Florida is dominated by a slow-moving river of grass: the Everglades.

The Everglades is not a swamp in the usual sense. It is a vast, shallow river of freshwater that flows slowly southward across the Florida peninsula from Lake Okeechobee toward Florida Bay.

This system is home to alligators, crocodiles, manatees, wading birds, and panthers. It is also a critical part of South Florida's water supply, recharging the and buffering hurricanes.

Florida is shaped by water in a way no other southeastern state is. Oceans on two sides. Lakes in the middle. Wetlands everywhere. Aquifers below. And hurricanes spinning in off warm Atlantic and Gulf currents.

State Spotlight

Virginia

A transition state that connects the coastal Southeast, the Appalachians, and the Mid-Atlantic.

Virginia stretches from the Atlantic in the east to the Blue Ridge and Appalachian regions in the west. Few states cover so many landscapes inside their borders.

The eastern includes the Chesapeake Bay, tidal rivers, and coastal wetlands. The middle of the state is rolling . The west rises into the Blue Ridge and the Valley and Ridge , with the Shenandoah Valley running between them.

Virginia's geography shaped its early history. Jamestown was founded along the James River because water access was essential for travel and trade. Tobacco plantations spread along tidal rivers because boats could load crops directly onto ocean-bound ships.

Major rivers: James, York, Rappahannock, Potomac, Shenandoah

State Spotlight

West Virginia

The most mountainous state in this lesson, defined by ridges, valleys, forests, and coal.

West Virginia lies almost entirely within the Appalachian , especially the Appalachian and the Ridge and Valley area. The land is steep ridges, narrow valleys, and forested mountains cut by deep rivers.

West Virginia separated from Virginia during the Civil War. Geography mattered. Western Virginia's mountain economy of small farms and timber differed from eastern Virginia's plantation economy. The mountains supported smaller farms, logging, and later coal mining.

Coal became central. Ancient plant material, buried in rock layers for hundreds of millions of years, became coal seams. The mountains made coal possible, and they made mining dangerous.

Major rivers: New, Kanawha, Monongahela, Ohio

State Spotlight

Kentucky

A crossroads of mountains, river valleys, limestone caves, and bluegrass pastures.

Kentucky sits at the meeting point of the Deep South, Appalachia, and the Midwest. Eastern Kentucky is mountainous. The famous Bluegrass in the north-central part of the state is rolling hills with deep, fertile soil that supports horse farms and pastures. Western Kentucky reaches the Mississippi.

Kentucky is also famous for , a landscape formed when groundwater slowly dissolves limestone. Karst creates caves, sinkholes, springs, and underground rivers. Mammoth Cave in Kentucky is the longest known cave system on Earth.

The Cumberland Gap, where Kentucky meets Tennessee and Virginia, was one of the most important pioneer routes through the Appalachians. Settlers used it to push west into the interior.

Major rivers: Ohio, Kentucky, Cumberland, Green, Tennessee

State Spotlight

Tennessee

A long state with three grand divisions: East, Middle, and West, each with its own geography.

Tennessee is a long state, and its geography changes dramatically as you cross it east to west.

  • East Tennessee: The Great Smoky Mountains and Blue Ridge.
  • Cumberland : A high, flat tableland of forest and rock.
  • Central Basin and Highland Rim: Rolling pastureland centered on Nashville.
  • West Tennessee: Flat lowlands sloping toward the Mississippi River and Memphis.

The Tennessee River loops through several states and has been engineered with dams and locks by the Tennessee Valley Authority since the 1930s. Those projects brought electricity, flood control, and navigation to the entire valley.

East Tennessee's mountain culture has long differed from West Tennessee's cotton-and-Mississippi-River culture. One state, three different worlds.

State Spotlight

North Carolina

A classic mountain-to-sea state, with three distinct regions and famous barrier islands.

North Carolina has three major geographic zones: mountains in the west, in the middle, and in the east. The state is a textbook example of how the Southeast slopes from highlands toward the Atlantic.

The mountains include parts of the Blue Ridge and Great Smoky Mountains. The middle Piedmont holds Charlotte, the Research Triangle, and most of the state's universities and industry. The east opens onto wetlands, sounds, and the famous Outer Banks.

The Outer Banks are a chain of barrier islands. They shelter the mainland from storms but are constantly reshaped by waves and currents. North Carolina's shallow sounds made it hard to build large port cities, but its mountains, Piedmont cities, and beaches all attract visitors today.

Major rivers: Cape Fear, Neuse, Roanoke, Yadkin-Pee Dee, Tar

State Spotlight

South Carolina

A state of contrasts: Upcountry hills in the northwest and Lowcountry marshes along the coast.

South Carolina slopes from a small slice of Blue Ridge in the far northwest, through the upstate, down to the and coast in the east and south.

The Lowcountry includes barrier islands, salt marshes, estuaries, sea islands, and tidal creeks. Charleston grew into a major port because of its harbor and coastal location. Tidal rivers along this coast supported rice plantations from the colonial era onward.

The Congaree in central South Carolina protects one of the largest bottomland hardwood forests left in the country.

Major rivers: Savannah, Santee, Pee Dee, Edisto, Congaree

State Spotlight

Georgia

A state that contains nearly every southeastern : mountains, , , and .

Georgia is one of the most geographically complete states in the Southeast. North Georgia has the Appalachian , Ridge and Valley, and Blue Ridge. Central Georgia is . South Georgia lies in the .

Georgia's runs diagonally across the state from Columbus through Macon to Augusta. Every one of those cities grew because of the falling rivers there.

Atlanta is unusual: it grew inland, not on a coast, because of transportation. It became a railroad hub in the 1800s, then a highway and airport hub. The mountains, climate, and Piedmont soils all shaped what Georgia grew and where Georgians lived.

Major rivers: Chattahoochee, Savannah, Flint, Altamaha, Ocmulgee, Oconee

State Spotlight

Florida

Florida is defined by water: oceans on two sides, aquifers below, wetlands across the middle, and hurricanes spinning in off the warm seas.

Florida is a peninsula. The Atlantic Ocean is on one side, the Gulf of Mexico on the other, and warm subtropical water surrounds it. The land is mostly low and flat compared to other southeastern states. Its highest natural point is just 345 feet above sea level.

Florida's geography includes the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, the Everglades, the Florida Keys, central Florida lakes, wetlands, springs, and barrier islands. Beneath all of this lies the Floridan , supplying most of the state's freshwater.

South Florida is closer to a true tropical climate. North Florida is like the rest of the Southeast. Hurricanes are a constant geographic hazard because Florida juts into the warmest hurricane-producing waters in the country.

Major water features: St. Johns River, Suwannee River, Apalachicola River, Lake Okeechobee, the Everglades, Florida Keys

State Spotlight

Alabama

Rivers, minerals, and the rich dark soil of the Black Belt shaped Alabama's economy.

Alabama covers a wide range of geography: Appalachian foothills in the north, the Cumberland , Ridge and Valley, , the famous Black Belt prairie, the , and a short stretch of Gulf Coast at Mobile.

The Black Belt is a long arc of dark, fertile soil that runs through central Alabama and into Mississippi. That soil made the a center of cotton agriculture, which was tied directly to enslaved labor before the Civil War.

Birmingham grew because of geography too. Northern Alabama happened to have coal, iron ore, and limestone all within a short distance of each other. Those three minerals are what you need to make steel. Birmingham became the South's iron and steel capital.

Major rivers: Alabama, Tombigbee, Coosa, Tallapoosa, Tennessee, Chattahoochee

State Spotlight

Mississippi

A state shaped by the Mississippi River and the dark, fertile floodplains it left behind.

Mississippi has two major geographic identities: the eastern and central uplands, and the flat, fertile Mississippi in the west between the Mississippi and Yazoo Rivers.

Notice the wording. The "Mississippi Delta" inside the state of Mississippi is the , not the actual river mouth. The river's true delta, where it meets the Gulf, is in Louisiana.

The Delta's rich alluvial soil made it one of the most important cotton-growing regions in the entire country. That soil also tied the region tightly to slavery, plantation agriculture, sharecropping after the Civil War, and the cultural roots of blues music.

Major rivers: Mississippi, Yazoo, Pearl, Big Black, Tombigbee

State Spotlight

Arkansas

Mountains, river valleys, and Mississippi lowlands all meet inside Arkansas.

Arkansas is geographically diverse in ways many people do not expect. It includes the Ozark in the north, the Ouachita Mountains in the west, the Arkansas River Valley running across the state, the Mississippi Alluvial Plain in the east, and the West Gulf in the south.

This makes Arkansas a bridge between the Southeast, the Midwest, and the Great Plains. Eastern Arkansas, with its flat Mississippi River lowlands, developed plantation agriculture. Western and northern Arkansas, with mountains and hills, developed smaller farms, timber, mining, and tourism.

Major rivers: Arkansas, Mississippi, White, Ouachita, Red, St. Francis

State Spotlight

Louisiana

A state. Its land was built by rivers, and its future depends on water, , storms, and sea level.

Louisiana is one of the most water-shaped states in the country. The Mississippi River , coastal marshes, swamps, natural levees, bayous, barrier islands, and prairies are all part of its landscape.

New Orleans grew where it did because it controlled trade between the interior of North America and the Gulf of Mexico. Anything floating down the Mississippi had to pass through it. That location brought wealth and strategic importance, but also serious flood risk that continues to this day.

Louisiana's wetlands protect inland areas from storms, support fisheries, and provide wildlife habitat. But the state is losing coastal land. Subsidence, levees that prevent from reaching the wetlands, canals dug for oil and gas, and hurricanes have all reduced the marshes.

Major rivers and waters: Mississippi, Red, Atchafalaya, Ouachita, Pearl, Lake Pontchartrain, Gulf of Mexico

Putting It Together

Big Patterns Across the Southeast

Step back, and the Southeast reveals a handful of patterns that repeat across nearly every state.
  1. Mountains in the north and west, plains toward the coast. The land slopes from highlands down toward the Atlantic Ocean or Gulf of Mexico. Rivers run downhill, carrying toward the sea.
  2. Rivers became transportation corridors. Before railroads, rivers moved everything. Cities grew where rivers met oceans, where rivers crossed the , or where river valleys cut routes through mountains.
  3. Soil shaped agriculture. soils produced cotton and soybeans. soils grew pine, peanuts, and tobacco. Limestone Bluegrass soils raised horses. Mountain soils supported smaller farms and orchards.
  4. Coasts brought both opportunity and danger. Ports, tourism, fishing, and trade depend on the coast. So does hurricane damage, , flooding, and sea-level risk.
  5. Geography created regional differences inside states. East Tennessee feels different from West Tennessee. North Georgia from South Georgia. Mountain Virginia from Virginia. The land made these differences.
Reference

Glossary

Click any underlined word in the lesson above to see its meaning. The full list is collected here for quick review.

Region

/ REE-jun /

An area that shares certain characteristics like climate, landforms, or culture.

Landform

/ LAND-form /

A natural feature of Earth's surface, such as a mountain, valley, plain, plateau, or delta.

Coastal Plain

/ KOH-stuhl PLAYN /

Low, relatively flat land near an ocean or gulf.

Piedmont

/ PEED-mont /

A rolling upland region between mountains and coastal plains. The word literally means 'foot of the mountain.'

Fall Line

/ FAWL LYNE /

The boundary where harder upland rocks meet softer coastal plain sediments, often creating waterfalls or rapids.

Delta

/ DEL-tuh /

Land built by sediment deposited at the mouth of a river.

Aquifer

/ AK-wuh-fer /

An underground layer of rock or sediment that stores groundwater.

Wetland

/ WET-land /

Land covered or soaked by water for at least part of the year.

Barrier Island

/ BAYR-ee-er EYE-luhnd /

A long, narrow island parallel to the coast that helps protect the mainland from waves and storms.

Floodplain

/ FLUD-playn /

Flat land near a river that can flood when the river rises.

Karst

/ KARST /

A landscape formed when water dissolves rock such as limestone, creating caves, sinkholes, and underground streams.

Humid Subtropical

/ HYOO-mid sub-TROP-ih-kul /

A climate with hot summers, mild winters, and regular rainfall.

Estuary

/ ES-choo-air-ee /

A coastal area where freshwater from rivers mixes with salt water from the ocean.

Tidewater

/ TYDE-waw-ter /

Low coastal land affected by ocean tides, especially in Virginia and the Carolinas.

Bayou

/ BYE-yoo /

A slow-moving creek or swampy section of a river, especially in Louisiana.

Plateau

/ pla-TOH /

A large area of high, relatively flat land.

Sediment

/ SED-uh-ment /

Tiny pieces of rock, soil, or organic material carried and deposited by water, wind, or ice.

Erosion

/ ee-ROH-zhun /

The slow wearing away of land by water, wind, or ice.
